topic: The Physics of Pi: Colliding Blocks and Digits
target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school physics enthusiasts

sections.title: The Hook: Counting Collisions
sections.content: Introduce the counter-intuitive phenomenon: when two blocks of mass m and M (where M = 100^n * m) collide elastically, the total number of collisions between the blocks and a wall is exactly the first n digits of pi.
sections.example: Visualize two blocks: a small 'mouse' block (m=1kg) and a massive 'elephant' block (M=100kg) sliding on a frictionless surface towards a wall.

sections.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
sections.content: Briefly review elastic collisions. Emphasize that conservation of momentum (p=mv) and kinetic energy (KE=0.5mv^2) are the 'engine' driving the block interactions.
sections.example: Use a vector arrow animation showing the exchange of velocity between a stationary elephant block and an incoming mouse block.

sections.title: Mapping Physics to Geometry
sections.content: Introduce the 'Phase Space' concept. Map the velocities of the two blocks to the x and y axes of a coordinate system. The conservation of energy forms a circular arc in this plane; collisions become reflections off specific lines.
sections.example: A 2D graphical overlay showing a particle bouncing inside a triangular wedge, where the angle of the wedge is determined by the mass ratio M/m.

sections.title: The Emergence of Pi
sections.content: Connect the geometry to trigonometry. As the mass ratio becomes extremely large (M/m → ∞), the 'wedge' angle becomes very small, essentially 'unrolling' the reflections into a circular arc, directly linking the collision count to the circumference-to-diameter ratio.
sections.example: Animation showing the wedge angle shrinking as the elephant block grows; the total number of reflections approaches the arc length calculation of a circle, which equals π.

sections.title: Conclusion: Why does it happen?
sections.content: Summarize that pi is not 'hidden' in the blocks, but rather a property of circular rotation in phase space. Final takeaway: Physics laws often hide geometric truths in plain sight.
sections.example: A final visual showing the sequence '3', '1', '4' appearing on a digital counter as the blocks finish their dance.
